score.headline: A one-sided contract built entirely around the practice — stacked fees, no safety net, and covenants that could cost you well over $30,000 and lock you out of the whole metro for three years.

categories.rationale: The 22% rate is already low, and it's applied after an 8% management fee, lab costs, and chargebacks come out of collections first — so your effective take is closer to 15%. There is no daily guarantee at all, so you carry the entire risk of a slow ramp.

A 36-month, 25-mile non-compete measured from every affiliated location statewide, backed by $150,000 in liquidated damages plus the employer's legal fees, is among the most aggressive structures you'll see and could bar you from most of the metro for three years.

As a 1099 contractor you get no health insurance, no retirement, no PTO, and no CE — and you buy your own malpractice tail on the way out. Much of this stems from a worker classification that a fixed schedule and employer control may not support.

The employer can fire you instantly with no notice while you owe 120 days, a production quota converts a bad month into a for-cause exit, and binding arbitration with a class-action waiver strips your options if a dispute arises.

summary: This is a three-year independent-contractor offer from Apex Dental Management, a high-volume corporate group in Phoenix. You are paid 22% of collections — but only after an 8% management fee, lab costs, and insurance chargebacks are subtracted first — with no daily guarantee of any kind. It includes a $10,000 signing bonus repayable with interest for three years, a 36-month/25-mile non-compete measured from every affiliated office in the state with a $150,000 penalty, mandatory arbitration, no benefits, and provider-paid malpractice tail. As written, it places nearly all of the financial and legal risk on you.

red_flags.title: An 8% management fee comes out before your split
red_flags.explanation: On top of being paid on collections rather than production, an 8% 'practice management fee' and all lab costs are subtracted before your 22% is calculated. Stacked together, these deductions cut your effective share to roughly 15% of what you produce.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for the management fee to be removed from your compensation math and for the split to be based on production, or at minimum for lab fees to come out after your percentage.

red_flags.title: No daily guarantee of any kind
red_flags.explanation: There is no floor on your pay. During the months your schedule is still filling — often the first half-year — you are paid only your small percentage of whatever comes in, with nothing to cushion slow days.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for a daily or monthly guarantee for at least the first 6 months while you build a patient base.

red_flags.title: 36-month, 25-mile non-compete across every affiliate statewide
red_flags.explanation: The restriction applies for three years around any Apex-affiliated location in the state — not just where you worked. In a large metro that can blanket the entire area, effectively forcing you to leave the region to keep practicing.
red_flags.what_to_do: Insist on limiting the non-compete to your primary office, a shorter term (12-24 months), and a smaller radius — and have it reviewed for enforceability under Arizona law.

red_flags.title: $150,000 penalty plus the employer's legal fees for a breach
red_flags.explanation: Breaching the covenant triggers an automatic $150,000 payment and makes you pay Apex's attorney fees — a six-figure fixed penalty unrelated to any actual harm, designed to make leaving too risky to attempt.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask to strike the liquidated-damages and fee-shifting clauses entirely; they are not standard in associate agreements.

red_flags.title: You are classified as a 1099 contractor with none of the control
red_flags.explanation: You get no benefits and owe self-employment tax, yet Apex sets your schedule, location, and protocols and requires on-call coverage — the hallmarks of an employee. Misclassification shifts thousands in taxes and benefits onto you and can create legal exposure for both sides.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask to be classified as a W-2 employee, or to have the pay raised substantially to offset the taxes and benefits you must now cover yourself.

red_flags.title: Indefinite chargebacks for refunds and insurance takebacks
red_flags.explanation: If a patient is refunded or an insurer claws money back — even years later, and even on work you were already paid for — the amount is deducted from your future pay with no time limit.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for a cap and a time limit on chargebacks, and to exclude takebacks caused by the office's own billing errors.

red_flags.title: Production quota converts a slow month into a firing
red_flags.explanation: Missing a $3,000/day production target in any two months is grounds for immediate for-cause termination — turning a normal slow stretch into a job loss, and a for-cause one that's harder to explain to the next employer.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask to remove the hard quota, or replace it with a good-faith review and a cure period before any termination.

red_flags.title: Binding arbitration with a class-action waiver
red_flags.explanation: Any dispute must go to private arbitration in Apex's home county, and you waive the right to join with other associates in a class action. This quietly removes most of your practical leverage if something goes wrong.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask to keep access to the courts, or at minimum for a neutral venue and shared arbitration costs.

red_flags.title: Zero notice from them, 120 days from you
red_flags.explanation: Apex can end the agreement immediately, but you must give four months' notice or be in breach — a lopsided arrangement that keeps you locked in while leaving you exposed.
red_flags.what_to_do: Ask for mutual notice periods of 60-90 days.

negotiation_email:
Subject: Apex associate agreement — a few things to work through before I sign

Hi [Name],

Thank you for the offer to join the Phoenix team — I'm excited about the patient volume and the chance to build my clinical speed early. I've read the agreement closely, and there are a few structural items I'd want to resolve before signing:

1. Compensation. As drafted, my 22% is calculated after an 8% management fee and lab costs come out of collections, which puts my effective share around 15%. Could we base the split on production and remove the management fee from that math? Seeing the office's collection history would help me plan realistically.

2. Classification. Given the set schedule and on-call requirements, could this be a W-2 role — or the rate adjusted to reflect the taxes and benefits I'd be covering as a 1099 contractor?

3. Non-compete. The current 36-month, 25-mile restriction across every affiliate statewide, with a $150,000 penalty, is broader than I can accept. Could we limit it to my primary location, shorten the term, and remove the liquidated-damages clause?

4. Ramp-up. Since a new associate's schedule takes time to fill, would you add a daily guarantee for the first six months?

I'm genuinely interested in making this work, and I'd rather get the structure right up front than run into surprises later. Happy to talk any of this through by phone.

Best,
[Name]
value_at_stake: Fixing even the compensation structure and the non-compete on this offer is worth well over $30,000 a year plus your freedom to keep working locally — the difference between a viable job and one to walk away from.
overall_read: This is a materially one-sided agreement. A low collections-based rate is stacked with an 8% management fee and lab deductions, there is no guarantee, benefits are nonexistent under a questionable 1099 classification, and the covenants — a three-year statewide non-compete with a $150,000 penalty — are built to make leaving prohibitively expensive. Some of these terms are negotiable and some may not be enforceable, but as written this contract asks you to carry nearly all of the risk. If the practice won't move on the compensation structure and the non-compete, this is an offer worth walking away from.
